qs.q: A 32-year-old agricultural worker in Southeast Asia presents with high fever, severe headache, myalgias, and a prominent dark lesion with a central black crust on his thigh. Epidemiological investigation confirms a diagnosis of scrub typhus. Which arthropod genus serves as the primary vector for this pathogen?
qs.e: Orientia tsutsugamushi, the causative agent of scrub typhus, is transmitted by the bite of larval Leptotrombidium mites (chiggers). Dermacentor variabilis is a tick vector that transmits Rickettsia rickettsii, the cause of Rocky Mountain spotted fever, rather than scrub typhus.

qs.q: In the transmission cycle of scrub typhus, what unique biological feature allows Leptotrombidium mites to perpetuate the pathogen without needing a new mammalian host every generation?
qs.e: Orientia tsutsugamushi is maintained in Leptotrombidium mite populations through transovarial transmission from infected female mites to their offspring. This allows the mite population to act as both vector and reservoir.

qs.q: Epidemic typhus and Chagas disease can both be vectored via
qs.e: Both diseases are transmitted by the faeces (frass) of the vector, which is rubbed into the bite or the skin.

qs.q: Which one of the following genera is a biological vector of scrub typhus pathogens?
qs.e: Leptotrombidium mites (chiggers) are the biological vectors of Orientia tsutsugamushi, the causative agent of scrub typhus. The mites serve as both vector and reservoir, with transovarial transmission maintaining the pathogen in mite populations.

ai.title: Typhus
ai.subject: Microbiology & immunology
ai.summary: Typhus is a rickettsial infection transmitted by lice, fleas or ticks, presenting with high fever, rash and often an eschar. Rapid diagnosis and doxycycline treatment are lifesaving, especially in low‑resource settings.

sections.p: Typhus refers to several rickettsial diseases caused by Rickettsia prowazekii, Rickettsia typhi and Rickettsia tsutsugamushi/Orientia tsutsugamushi. They share a common clinical picture of abrupt high fever, headache, myalgia and a characteristic rash, but differ in vector, geographic distribution and specific signs such as eschar.
Rickettsiae are obligate intracellular gram‑negative bacteria that invade endothelial cells, causing vasculitis. They are transmitted by arthropod vectors and can survive in the host for weeks.

Transmission depends on the species: R. prowazekii via body lice, R. typhi via fleas (cat/dog), and R. tsutsugamushi via chigger mites. In low‑resource hospitals, overcrowding and poor sanitation increase louse exposure.

All typhus forms present with sudden high fever, headache, myalgia and a diffuse rash that may start on the trunk and spread to extremities. Scrub typhus uniquely shows an eschar at the bite site. Severe complications include ARDS, renal failure and shock.

Clinical suspicion is key. Confirmatory tests include Weil‑Felix agglutination (for murine typhus) and indirect immunofluorescence or PCR (for scrub typhus). In many East African centres, only basic serology or a presumptive diagnosis is possible.

t.b: Positive agglutination with OX19/OX2 indicates murine typhus; a titer ≥1:160 supports diagnosis.
Detects specific IgM/IgG against Rickettsia; a rise in titre over 4 days confirms infection.
Detects rickettsial DNA in blood or eschar; a positive result is definitive but often unavailable.
High fever >3 days, rash, and exposure history; if present, start treatment empirically.

sections.p: Remember that typhus presents with a rash that starts on the trunk and spreads to extremities, often with an eschar in scrub typhus. In low‑resource settings, a positive Weil‑Felix or a presumptive clinical diagnosis warrants immediate doxycycline. Avoid macrolides in murine typhus due to resistance.
Typhoid fever (Salmonella Typhi) and malaria can mimic typhus. Typhoid has a sustained fever and rose‑spot rash, while malaria shows cyclical fevers and splenomegaly.

Weil‑Felix may give false positives in endemic areas; a negative result does not rule out typhus. PCR requires specialised labs; a negative PCR in a high‑pretest‑probability patient still needs treatment.
Urgent care is needed if the patient develops respiratory distress, altered mental status, hypotension, or signs of organ failure.

faq.q: What is the most common vector for epidemic typhus?
Why is doxycycline the drug of choice?
faq.a: It penetrates endothelial cells and is effective against all rickettsial species

faq.q: Can typhus be transmitted by mosquitoes?
faq.a: No, rickettsiae are not transmitted by mosquitoes

exam: A 25‑year‑old man presents with sudden high fever, headache and a macular rash that started on the trunk. He works in a crowded dormitory. What is the first step in management? — Start doxycycline immediately; consider a presumptive diagnosis if tests are unavailable.
A patient with suspected typhus has a negative Weil‑Felix test. What should you do? — Treat empirically with doxycycline; repeat serology in 7–10 days.
Why is azithromycin preferred in children under 8? — Doxycycline is contraindicated in young children due to teeth discoloration.
What distinguishes scrub typhus from murine typhus? — Presence of an eschar at the bite site in scrub typhus.
A patient with typhus develops acute kidney injury. What complication should you monitor for? — Acute tubular necrosis and acute respiratory distress syndrome.
Why should you avoid macrolides for murine typhus? — They are ineffective against Rickettsia typhi.
What is the typical rash distribution in typhus? — Begins on the trunk and spreads to extremities, sparing palms and soles.
